title: Buyer overpays with a check
setup: You listed your couch for $300. A buyer says they're relocating for work.

messages.text: I'll take it! My assistant mailed you a cashier's check for $1,800. It includes my movers' fee.
Please deposit it and send the extra $1,500 to the movers by payment app so they can pick it up tomorrow.

options.label: Deposit the check, then send the $1,500
options.feedback: The check bounced weeks later. The bank took back the money, and your $1,500 was gone.

options.label: Say no. Local pickup, exact amount, cash or in-app payment only
options.feedback: No real buyer overpays and asks for change back. Keeping it simple and local shuts the scam down.

options.label: Wait until the check “clears,” then send the money
options.feedback: Funds can show as available before a fake check is caught. When it bounced, you owed the bank.

redFlags: Check for more than the price
Asks you to send the difference to someone else
Buyer can't meet in person
safestAction: Never accept overpayment. If a check is involved, don't send any money back — ever.

title: “Upgrade your account to receive payment”
setup: You're selling a camera. The buyer says they paid and to check your email.

content.subject: Pending payment of $450.00 — action required
content.body:
A payment of $450.00 has been sent to you but is on hold because your account is not a Business account.

To release funds, the buyer must pay an extra $300 upgrade fee, or you may pay it yourself and be refunded instantly with your payment.

options.label: Pay the $300 upgrade — you'll get it back
options.feedback: There was never a payment. The “upgrade fee” went to the fake buyer.

options.label: Open your payment app yourself and check your balance
options.feedback: No pending money appeared in your real app, because there wasn't any. Payment services don't email from Gmail.

options.label: Ship the camera since the email says they paid
options.feedback: The payment email was fake. You lost the camera and never got paid.

redFlags: Payment company emailing from a Gmail address
Pay a fee to receive money
Buyer pushes you to check email instead of your app
safestAction: Confirm payments only inside your payment app. You never pay to receive money.

title: Too-good-to-be-true clearance ad
setup: Scrolling social media, you see an ad for a vacuum you've wanted.

content.body: 🔥 WAREHOUSE CLEARANCE 🔥 Premium cordless vacuums, normally $649, now just $49! Only 12 left. Ends tonight!
content.subject: Premium Cordless Vacuum — 92% OFF

options.label: Order it before they sell out
options.feedback: No vacuum arrived. The site kept your card and ran more charges.

options.label: Skip it. Search the store's name + “scam” or “reviews” first
options.feedback: A quick search usually shows complaints about sites like this. 92% off with comments turned off is a classic fake store.

options.label: Buy it, but pay with a gift card for privacy
options.feedback: Paying a fake store with a gift card means no chance of getting it back.

redFlags: Unrealistic discount
Countdown and “only 12 left” pressure
Comments turned off; odd .shop domain
safestAction: Research unfamiliar stores before buying and pay by credit card, which offers the strongest dispute rights.

title: Buyer wants to meet at the police station
setup: You're selling a used tablet for $180. A local buyer writes.

messages.text: Hi, is the tablet available? I can do $180 cash.
Could we meet at the safe exchange spot in the police station parking lot Saturday at noon? I'd like to power it on before I pay.

options.label: Agree. Meet there, let him test it, count the cash
options.feedback: Local buyer, established profile, public safe-exchange spot, full price in person. That's how it should go.

options.label: Decline — it seems too easy
options.feedback: No harm done, but this was a real, careful buyer. You're still stuck with the tablet.

options.label: Ask him to pay a deposit first by gift card
options.feedback: Asking a real buyer for gift cards looks like a scam — and scared him off.

redFlags: Meets in person at a public, monitored place
Pays the asking price, no overpayment
Established profile with ratings
safestAction: For local sales, meet in a public place (many police stations have safe-exchange zones) and accept cash or in-app payment in person.

title: Dream apartment, landlord out of the country
setup: You're apartment hunting. A two-bedroom in a great neighborhood is listed for well under market rent.

messages.text: God bless. I'm doing missionary work overseas, so I can't show the unit. Many people want it.
Send the $1,150 deposit and first month by payment app and I will mail you the keys right away.

options.label: Send the $2,300 before someone else gets it
options.feedback: The listing was copied from a real rental. No keys ever came, and the owner didn't know it was listed.

options.label: Insist on seeing it in person and verifying who owns it before paying anything
options.feedback: Real landlords let you see the place. Checking property records or meeting in person exposes fake listings fast.

options.label: Send just the deposit to hold it
options.feedback: Any money sent to hold an unseen rental can vanish. The deposit was gone.

redFlags: Rent far below similar units
Landlord can't meet or show the property
Wants money by payment app or wire before you see it
safestAction: Never pay for a rental you haven't seen. Search the address to see if the listing appears elsewhere under a different name.

title: Refund confirmation for your return
setup: Last week you returned a jacket at the store's counter. Today:

content.subject: Your refund has been issued
content.body:
Hi Sam,

We've received your return of Men's Alpine Jacket (Order #NL-448120). A refund of $129.00 has been issued to your Visa ending in 1188. Please allow 5–10 business days for it to appear.

No action is needed.
content.footer: Questions? Visit northline.com/help or call the number on your receipt.

options.label: Nothing to do. Watch your card statement for the refund
options.feedback: Matches a return you made, uses your name, and asks for nothing. That's what a real refund notice looks like.

options.label: Call the store to “confirm” by giving your full card number
options.feedback: It was real, so nothing bad happened. But no store needs your full card number to issue a refund.

options.label: Mark it as spam
options.feedback: No harm, but this one was legitimate, and future messages from the store may get lost.

redFlags: Matches a return you actually made
Addresses you by name with order details
“No action is needed” — no link or request
safestAction: Real notices match your activity and don't ask for anything. Confirm on your card statement or in your account.

title: QR menu at a restaurant table
setup: You sit down at a busy restaurant. A printed table card has a QR code. The server says, “Menu and ordering are on the code.”

content.subject: Scan for menu & ordering
content.sender: Printed into a laminated table card with the restaurant's logo

options.label: Check the preview, see it's the restaurant's site, and open the menu
options.feedback: The staff told you to use it, it's printed on their materials, and the preview matches the restaurant's name. Checking the preview is the right habit.

options.label: Refuse to scan and ask for a paper menu
options.feedback: Totally fine and never wrong, but this one was legitimate. Checking the link preview works too.

options.label: Scan it and enter your card without looking at the link
options.feedback: It happened to be real, but skipping the preview is how parking and package QR scams get people.

redFlags: Printed on the restaurant's own table card, not a stuck-on sticker
Staff directed you to it
Link preview matches the restaurant's name
safestAction: Before tapping any QR link, read the preview. Make sure it matches who you expect and has no odd spellings.
